columns.label: Ebook
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily get and consume ebooks on the platform (free or paid) as a first-class product, open, buy, borrow, or read without hunting.

columns.label: Short-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily consume short-form video as a first-class surface (For You, Reels, Shorts).

columns.label: Long-form video
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch creator / UGC long-form video (or specialty long video) as a core surface. Course lectures belong under Courses. Hollywood catalogs belong under Series/Films.

columns.label: Series/Films
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily watch series and films as an SVOD / catalog entertainment product.

columns.label: Courses
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily take or browse structured courses as a first-class product.

columns.label: Newsletters
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily read or subscribe to newsletters / creator writing as a first-class product.

columns.label: Audio
columns.definition: Yes if you can easily listen to music, podcasts, or audiobooks as a first-class product.

columns.label: Memberships
columns.definition: Yes if a creator or seller can accept payments from others and make money through the platform, checkout, fan subscriptions, tips, ads, shop, or creator funds. Not only a classic Patreon-style membership product.

columns.label: Community & Messaging
columns.definition: Yes if you can create or join a group, community, or club, including group chats, Groups, subreddits, community tabs, discussion boards, or community feeds. A one-off comment on a single video or listing is not the bar; a durable place for the group to talk is.

columns.label: Storefronts
columns.definition: Yes if the product gives a creator a custom storefront or site that can take the place of building their own website (bio page, creator site, branded shop). Not a shop tab on someone else’s multi-seller marketplace.

columns.label: Marketplaces
columns.definition: Yes if a typical person can search and shop a catalog of offerings from many sellers, courses, books, digital goods, etc. Storefront software (Shopify, WooCommerce) is not a marketplace unless shoppers browse many sellers there.

scaleFacts: SaaS focused on memberships layered on existing websites (WordPress, Ghost, custom sites).
Pricing (2026): Standard ≈USD 49/month + ≈4.9% transaction fee; Test Mode free (Stripe test payments only); Enterprise custom/volume fees.
Requires creator’s own Stripe account; Stripe fees ≈2.9% + USD 0.30 per US card transaction on top of Memberful’s fee.

strengths.title: Flexible membership models
strengths.detail: Monthly, annual, pay-what-you-want, custom recurring intervals, plus one-time purchases (courses, ebooks, downloads).

strengths.title: Multiple monetization options
strengths.detail: Memberships, private podcasts, newsletters (via email integrations), digital downloads, and member-only page/post/forum access.

strengths.title: Full control over Stripe and audience
strengths.detail: Creators connect their own Stripe account; own payment data and customer relationships; can export data including Stripe Customer IDs.

strengths.title: Website-centric approach
strengths.detail: Works with WordPress, Ghost, and custom sites; WordPress plugin for content protection and branded checkout; basic website builder.

weaknesses.title: High total fee burden
weaknesses.detail: USD 49/month + ≈4.9% platform + Stripe ≈2.9%+0.30, effective fees can easily exceed 7–8% per sale.

weaknesses.title: No built-in email, courses, or community
weaknesses.detail: Needs external tools for email marketing, course delivery, and community (ConvertKit, forums, Discord, etc.).

weaknesses.title: WordPress dependency for full power
weaknesses.detail: Many advanced use cases assume WordPress; non-WordPress setups can be more complex or limited.

weaknesses.title: Complexity for non-technical users
weaknesses.detail: More configuration than plug-and-play platforms like Patreon, protecting content and integrating sites takes work.

content:
Kahana is a library of curated hubs, Explore, Clubs, and optional Stripe. Memberful is recurring membership, patronage, or exclusive fan content. They overlap in places and diverge in others.

What each one is

Kahana is built around hubs people can open, Explore so strangers can find them, Aura as scarce daily recognition, and Clubs so discussion outlives a feed. Selling stays optional.

Memberful provides every tool you need to sell memberships, courses, digital downloads, newsletters, and private podcasts, all while keeping full control of your audience and Stripe account.

Why this comparison

This article puts Kahana and Memberful side by side. It covers what each supports as a first-class product job, key features, and a few research notes so you have a clearer picture of what they are, how they compare, and what you can actually do on each one. It is not a teardown, and it is not a switch-tomorrow pitch.
contentAfter:
What you can do on each

On Kahana you can publish a hub, list it on Explore, discuss it in a Club, grant Aura, and turn on a Stripe paywall when you are ready to charge.

On Memberful you can use Memberships as a first-class product job. Fans already live on that membership surface and prefer tiers, posts, or patronage-native extras.

Using Kahana with Memberful

You can use both. Memberful keeps doing what it already does well. Kahana is another place to package the work, get discovered, and grow an audience.

Keep patronage-native fans on Memberful. Dual-list related work on Kahana so people who browse libraries can find it, join a Club, and pay there too without rebuilding your whole fan stack.
